name: Fish-scale pearlescent lipstick

card.summary: Lip color containing guanine crystals from fish scales, which give a pearly shimmer that makes lips look fuller and glossier.
card.note: Guanine is an irritant to eyes in hazard data; many modern shimmer products use mica or synthetic pigments instead.

quick.overview:
Fish-scale pearlescent lipstick uses guanine, the crystalline purine found in fish skin cells, as a pearlescent pigment. The flat plate-like crystals reflect light in layers, producing a soft pearl sheen that can make lips look plumper and more luminous.

The pigment has a long history: 'pearl essence' was extracted from fish scales in Paris in 1656, and guanine was identified as its active substance in 1861. It is used in cosmetics such as eye shadow and nail polish, with mica and other pigments as common alternatives.
quick.how: People apply it as an ordinary lipstick, gloss or shimmer topper, often over a base color to add dimension in the center of the lips. Products may list guanine, sometimes as 'pearl essence' or 'fish scale'.
quick.risks: Reference sources note guanine may irritate the eyes. As an animal-derived ingredient it is avoided by vegans and people avoiding fish products. Anyone with fish allergy or lip sensitivity may wish to read ingredient lists.

lead: Fish-scale pearlescent lipstick refers to lip products that use guanine crystals harvested from fish scales as a shimmer pigment. Guanine occurs in specialised skin cells called iridocytes; the crystals form flat, diamond-shaped, multilayered plates, and light partly reflecting and partly passing between the layers creates a pearly luster.[1] On lips, that luster is used to give a glossy, fuller-looking finish.

Natural 'pearl essence' has a documented history: in 1656 in Paris a Mr. Jaquin extracted it from the scales of the common bleak, and in 1861 Charles-Louis Barreswil showed it was guanine.[1] Crystalline guanine is used in products such as shampoos, eye shadow and nail polish, and in simulated pearls and metallic paints. Alternatives for pearly effects include mica, ground-shell faux pearl and aluminum or bronze particles.[1]

angle.text: The pigment adds a light-reflecting sheen to lip color. Wearers use it to make lips look plumper and glossier, applied alone or over lipstick.

paras: Guanine is a purine base also found in DNA and RNA; here it matters as a crystal. In fish, stacked transparent plates produce the silvery iridescence of scales.[1][2] Cosmetic chemists use this property as pearlescent pigment.
Hazard data cited in reference sources list guanine as an eye irritant and non-flammable.[1] Guanine is insoluble in water.[2]

timeline.event: Pearl essence extracted from bleak scales in Paris.[1]
Guanine first isolated from guano by Julius Bodo Unger.[2]
Pearl essence shown to be guanine.[1]
